passages.happening:
‘This is what happened in the days of Xerxes, who reigned over 127 provinces from India to Cush’ (verse 1). He sits on his royal throne in the citadel of Susa, and in the third year of his reign he holds a feast for his officials, the military leaders of Persia and Media, and the nobles of the provinces.

‘And for a full 180 days he displayed the glorious riches of his kingdom and the magnificent splendor of his greatness’ (verse 4). Then he holds a seven-day feast in the palace garden court for everyone in the citadel, ‘from the least to the greatest’ (verse 5). There are linen hangings in white and blue, marble pillars, gold and silver couches on a mosaic floor, and wine in gold goblets, no two alike. ‘By order of the king, no limit was placed on the drinking’ (verse 8).

‘Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Xerxes’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The book opens far from Jerusalem, in the palace of the Persian king. Its first readers knew that many Jews still lived in the eastern provinces, decades after Cyrus let the exiles go home. Yet no Jew appears in this chapter, and God is not mentioned.

Xerxes I ruled Persia from about 486 to 465 BC. The Hebrew text calls him Ahasuerus, a form of his Persian name; Xerxes is the Greek form. His empire stretched from the Indus valley, India in verse 1, to the upper Nile, Cush. The 127 provinces are smaller districts than the great satrapies Greek writers describe. Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran, was one of the royal capitals, and French excavations there uncovered the palace complex with its great columned audience hall.

The third year of Xerxes was about 483 BC. Herodotus records that Xerxes gathered his leading men in the years before his invasion of Greece, which began in 480 BC, and some readers connect this long display with those plans, though the text does not say so.

Royal banquets were a way for ancient kings to show their power, reward loyalty and bind the nobles to the throne. The luxury described here matches what the Persian court was famous for. Guests reclined on couches to eat. And the word for feast, mishteh, comes from the verb to drink. The banquets of this chapter are the first of many in the book, and the plot will turn at them.
passages.later:
Daniel also lived under Persian kings and their unchangeable laws: ‘in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed’ (Daniel 6:8).

And Ezra names the same king briefly, at the start of his reign: ‘At the beginning of the reign of Xerxes, an accusation was lodged against the people of Judah and Jerusalem’ (Ezra 4:6).
passages.asks: The chapter piles up gold, silver and wine to show a king's greatness. Ask what you put on display to show that you matter. And ask where you have seen God at work in a story that, at first, seemed to have nothing to do with him.

passages.t: A queen who would not come
passages.happening:
On the seventh day, ‘when the king’s heart was merry with wine’ (verse 10), he orders seven eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti before him, ‘wearing her royal crown, to display her beauty to the people and officials. For she was beautiful to behold’ (verse 11).

‘Queen Vashti, however, refused to come at the king’s command brought by his eunuchs. And the king became furious, and his anger burned within him’ (verse 12).

The king asks his wise men what the law says should be done. Memucan, one of the seven princes, answers that the queen has wronged not only the king but every prince and people in the empire, because every wife will hear of it and despise her husband (verses 16-18). He advises a royal decree, recorded in the laws of Persia and Media ‘so that it cannot be repealed’ (verse 19), that Vashti shall never again come before the king, and that her royal position be given to another.

The king agrees. He sends letters to every province, ‘to each province in its own script and to each people in their own language, proclaiming that every man should be master of his own household’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is a carefully told story with a strong note of satire. It opens with vast numbers and piles up luxury, and then shows the most powerful man in the world unable to command his own wife. The king who displays the riches of his kingdom cannot control his temper, and his answer to one woman's refusal is a decree for the whole empire. Memucan turns a private embarrassment into a threat to every household.

The Persian king was surrounded by layers of access. Eunuchs, castrated male servants, attended him and the royal women. The seven princes who had personal access to the king formed an inner council. A queen appeared before the king's male guests only at his command, and his demand that Vashti show herself, wearing her crown, treated her as one more of his possessions on show.

Verse 19 brings in something the book will return to: a decree recorded among the laws of the Persians and the Medes could not be revoked. And the letters in every script and language reflect the empire's real government in many tongues, with Aramaic as the common language.

The word for law, dat, appears here for the first of about twenty times in the book.
passages.later: The book will come back to the law that cannot be repealed. When Haman's decree needs to be undone, the king says, ‘For a decree that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the royal signet ring cannot be revoked’ (8:8), and Daniel knows the same law (Daniel 6:8).
passages.hard:
Was Vashti right to refuse?

The text does not give her reasons, and it does not say whether she was right. Interpreters have seen her in two ways. Some see defiance of the king, which the book records as the event that sets the story moving. Others see a woman rightly refusing to be paraded before drunken men and degraded. Either way, her refusal costs her the crown, and the decree that follows says more about the king and his counselors than about her.

The book does not ask its readers to blame Vashti. It shows how easily power can be used against a woman who says no, and how quickly a powerful man's wounded pride can be written into law.

A word for anyone who is being pressured for sex, or for anything else, by someone with power over them: a boss, a teacher, a coach, a leader, an owner, a family member. You are not to blame for their pressure. Saying no is right, and it is not your fault if they punish you for it. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Vashti said no, and lost her crown, and the book does not condemn her. Ask whether you have ever punished someone for refusing what you had no right to demand. And ask how you treat those who have less power than you when they will not do what you want.
